headline: Sukuk trade below their own issuer's conventional curve
number: -18.6bp average across 18 issuers (median -8.7bp); 16 of 18 negative; 8 of 8 obligor groups negative on average (issuers grouped by the government backing them; Sharjah and the multilateral Arab Energy Fund stand alone).
interpretation: Holding the issuer fixed, investors accept a lower yield on sukuk.

headline: The discount is a sub-investment-grade phenomenon
number: Sub-IG issuers -50bp vs investment grade -5bp: gap -45bp, wild bootstrap p = 0.015 by obligor group. With a time-varying rule (government CDS above 150bp that month) the gap is -55bp (p = 0.077 by obligor group, 0.022 by issuer); with time-varying ratings (2 of 3 agencies below BBB-/Baa3, Dubai via its DEWA proxy) -58bp (p = 0.038; -56bp, p = 0.074, with Dubai excluded). Oman's discount narrowed by 21bp (90% CI [10.3, 32.4]) in the year after Moody's upgrade made it investment grade at two of three agencies.
interpretation: A threshold, not a smooth gradient: investment-grade issuers get single-digit discounts.

headline: Within the weakest sovereigns, the discount moves with credit risk
number: Oman -21.5bp and Bahrain -19.2bp per 100bp of CDS (Newey-West t -4.0, -3.0); also in monthly changes (-50.0, -21.2). For investment-grade issuers the within slope is +3.4bp.
interpretation: The pooled panel slope (-22.0bp) is not significant on its own once only six CDS series are counted (wild bootstrap p = 0.287); the case studies carry the claim.

headline: The discount exists at issue, not only in secondary quotes
number: Weak-credit sukuk priced a median -39.7bp against their issuer's conventional curve at issue, vs +19.8bp for the same issuers' new conventional bonds and -1.7bp for other issuers' sukuk; issuer-level correlation with the secondary basis 0.78.
interpretation: Stale secondary quotes cannot explain a discount that is already there on the pricing date.

headline: Sukuk quotes are somewhat stale, but that is not the story
number: Unchanged mid price on 7.9% of days for sukuk vs 1.5% for conventionals; sukuk absorb 0.47 of a conventional move on the day and 0.62 within a week (weak credits 0.56, KSA 0.89); 46% of the pooled same-month CDS effect reverses within six months (Bahrain: no reversal).
interpretation: Even after 120 business days sukuk move 0.83bp per conventional bp: damping is real, and stale quotes explain only part of the monthly CDS response.

headline: Mechanism: tenor and buy-and-hold demand, with modest evidence
number: Holm-adjusted p-values across the four mechanism tests (government-clustered wild bootstrap): CDS slope steepens by -2.1bp per 100bp per year of maturity (p 0.138); less liquid sukuk price richer, -0.81bp per bp of bid-ask gap (p 0.076); CDS x interbank spread -0.10 per bp (p 0.626); CDS x Ijara +10.9 (p 0.718), a low-power test because only 10 of the 68 twin sukuk are Ijara (43 are Hybrid).
interpretation: After the multiple-testing correction none clears 5%; the tenor and liquidity signs fit default/recovery pricing plus buy-and-hold demand. The Ijara test cannot rule asset backing in or out.

headline: Oil shocks do not move the basis directly
number: Median basis response to an oil-price rise +0.6bp at +5 days; the test could detect 3.1bp (+5) or 4.9bp (+20) with 80% power. Implied via credit: +0.71bp (90% CI [-0.82, 2.77]).
interpretation: Oil reaches the basis only through credit risk, and oil up-shocks in this sample raise GCC CDS (median +5.9bp at +5 days, placebo p < 0.001); several of them are regional conflicts.

headline: What it is worth
number: Bahrain about USD 45m a year; Sharjah about USD 27m a year; BAPCO Energies BSCC Closed about USD 11m a year (trailing-12-month basis x outstanding USD sukuk). Investment-grade sovereigns without USD sukuk (Kuwait, Abu Dhabi, UAE federal): predicted USD 0.3-1.3m per USD 1bn issued, intervals including zero.
interpretation: Sukuk issuance pays most for the weakest credits, which is where the discount sits.
